reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A rare, severe autosomal dominant metaphyseal dysplasia caused by activating variants in PTH1R, the parathyroid hormone/PTH-related peptide receptor
The receptor is constitutively active, producing biochemical hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia despite low or undetectable circulating parathyroid hormone
This PTH-independent hypercalcaemia is a key diagnostic clue distinguishing it from other metaphyseal dysplasias and from hyperparathyroidism
Presents with severe disproportionate short stature, marked limb deformity, joint contractures and a waddling gait
Radiographs show grossly expanded, ragged, cystic-appearing metaphyses that can mimic rickets or a metabolic bone disease
Craniofacial features include frontonasal prominence, hypertelorism, micrognathia and choanal stenosis
Nephrocalcinosis and hypercalciuria may complicate the chronic disturbance of calcium handling
reference.pathophysiology: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia results from dominant activating variants in PTH1R, which encodes the receptor shared by parathyroid hormone and PTH-related peptide. Constitutive, ligand-independent receptor signalling mimics persistent PTH and PTHrP action. In the growth plate, PTHrP signalling normally delays chondrocyte hypertrophy; its unregulated activation disrupts the orderly transition of proliferating to hypertrophic chondrocytes, producing the disorganised, expanded metaphyses. Systemically, the same overactive signalling drives bone resorption and renal calcium retention, causing hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia even though endogenous parathyroid hormone is appropriately suppressed.
additionalDifferentials: Metaphyseal dysplasia with other systemic features
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone demonstrating hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH
Skeletal survey showing expanded, ragged, cystic metaphyses
Renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and urine calcium excretion
Assessment for choanal stenosis and airway patency in infancy
redFlags: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia (dehydration, vomiting, altered consciousness) requiring urgent management
Nephrocalcinosis or renal impairment from chronic hypercalciuria
Airway compromise from choanal stenosis or craniofacial involvement in infancy
Severe progressive limb deformity limiting mobility
reference.prognosis: A severe dysplasia with marked short stature and deformity; the biochemical calcium disturbance may cause nephrocalcinosis and renal complications over time, but the metaphyseal changes tend to remodel toward maturity. Multidisciplinary metabolic and orthopaedic care is required.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the hypercalcaemia as hyperparathyroidism and pursuing parathyroid surgery
Diagnosing rickets on the radiographic appearance without checking calcium biochemistry
Missing nephrocalcinosis by omitting renal imaging
Overlooking choanal stenosis as a cause of neonatal respiratory difficulty
